lena.name: Dr. Lena Reyes
lena.role: field biologist (a scientist who studies animals in the wild)

case.title: Shells on the Cattails
case.hook: This week at the Field Station pond, I found dozens of little brown bug shapes hanging on the cattail stems. They don’t move at all. In the mud, my net caught something shaped a lot like them, but alive. And by the gate, a green case hangs under a milkweed leaf. A volunteer wrote on my jar: “Dead bugs?”
case.question: Are the shells on the cattails dead bugs, and what is the green case on the milkweed?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: A chrysalis isn’t a dead caterpillar. It’s the pupa stage: inside, the caterpillar’s body is being rebuilt into a butterfly.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: side by side
clues.t: A grasshopper nymph already looks like a small adult and grows by shedding its skin. A caterpillar looks nothing like its parent until after the chrysalis.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: close the circle
clues.t: Monarchs have 4 stages (complete metamorphosis). Grasshoppers have 3 (incomplete). Sea turtles and sunflowers have no metamorphosis.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: alike and different
clues.t: A dragonfly nymph lives underwater. Then it climbs a stem and sheds its skin one last time. The empty skin stays behind, and there’s no pupa.

solve.title: What did Dr. Reyes find?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: They’re all dead bugs. Something killed the insects at the pond.
options.why: Check Clue 4. The shells were empty, split down the back. Where did the insects go?

options.t: The shells are empty skins. Dragonfly nymphs climbed out of the water and shed their skin one last time to become adult dragonflies (incomplete: egg, nymph, adult). The green case is a monarch chrysalis (the pupa stage of complete metamorphosis), and a butterfly will come out.
options.why: Case cracked! Nothing died. Two insects, two kinds of metamorphosis. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

options.t: The shells and the green case come from the same kind of insect at the same stage.
options.why: Check Clues 2 and 3. Does a dragonfly have a chrysalis stage like the monarch?

nextup.title: What comes next?
todo: Look at the stage in the “Now” box.

why.t: A stage is one step in a life cycle. A monarch looks very different at each stage.

stages.alt: A tiny pale, ribbed monarch egg on a fuzzy milkweed leaf.
A monarch caterpillar with yellow, black and white stripes on a milkweed leaf.
A smooth green monarch chrysalis with gold dots, hanging from a stem.
An orange and black monarch butterfly hanging from a milkweed leaf.

whys: After about 4 days, a tiny caterpillar hatches. It eats its eggshell, then milkweed leaves.
After about two weeks of eating and growing, the caterpillar hangs upside down. Its skin splits and a green chrysalis is underneath.
About 10 days later, the chrysalis turns clear. An adult butterfly climbs out.
The adult lays eggs on milkweed, and the life cycle starts over.
nextup.q: Dr. Reyes’s chrysalis on the milkweed isn’t moving. What is happening inside?

opts.miss: Look at your strip. What comes after the chrysalis?

opts.t: It’s the pupa stage. The caterpillar is changing into a butterfly.
It’s a seed that will grow into milkweed.
opts.miss: Look at the strip. Which animal made the chrysalis?

nextup.win: The circle is complete! Egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly → eggs again. A still chrysalis is alive and changing. That’s a clue.

why.t: A big, slow Florida grasshopper. Its young are black with a yellow stripe. The adults are yellow and orange, with wings.

frames.alt: A monarch caterpillar on a milkweed leaf.
frames.note: It eats milkweed and sheds its skin as it grows. It looks nothing like a butterfly.
No eating, no walking. Inside, the body is being rebuilt.

why.t: A life cycle has no end. The adult makes offspring, and the offspring start the cycle over.

orgs.name: Monarch butterfly

stages.alt: A tiny pale, ribbed monarch egg on a fuzzy milkweed leaf.
A monarch caterpillar with yellow, black and white stripes on a milkweed leaf.
A smooth green monarch chrysalis with gold dots, hanging from a stem.
An orange and black monarch butterfly hanging from a milkweed leaf.

orgs.kindMiss: Count the stages. Is there a resting stage where the body changes completely?
orgs.why: Four very different stages, with a pupa (the chrysalis). The young looks nothing like the adult.

orgs.name: Grasshopper

stages.alt: A grasshopper pushing the end of its body into the soil to lay eggs.
A black lubber grasshopper nymph with no wings.
An adult lubber grasshopper with wings.

orgs.kindMiss: Count the stages. Does the nymph already look like a small adult?
orgs.why: Three stages and no pupa. The nymph looks like a small adult without wings.

orgs.name: Loggerhead sea turtle

stages.alt: Round white sea turtle eggs in a sandy nest.
A tiny dark loggerhead hatchling held in a gloved hand.
A young loggerhead sea turtle swimming.
A large adult loggerhead sea turtle swimming over a reef.

orgs.kindMiss: Does the hatchling change its body shape, or just grow bigger? And is a turtle an insect?
orgs.why: No metamorphosis. The hatchling is shaped like the adult and just grows. A loggerhead takes many years, often more than 20, to be ready to lay eggs.

orgs.name: Sunflower

stages.alt: Two sunflower seeds, one striped and one pale.
A small sunflower seedling with two round leaves in the soil.
A big yellow sunflower in bloom.
A dried sunflower head full of seeds, held in a hand.

orgs.why: Plants don’t have metamorphosis, but they have stages too. The flower makes seeds, and the seeds start the cycle again.

welcome.label: Welcome · shells on the cattails
welcome.script: Hi, it’s Dr. Reyes, down at the Field Station pond. Look at the jars in the case file. Dozens of little brown shells on the cattails, and none of them move. In the mud, something shaped just like them, but alive. And a green case on the milkweed. A volunteer thinks they’re dead bugs. Are they? Let’s find out.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · what comes next? (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Here’s my favorite insect to watch grow up: the monarch. Look at the stage in the Now box, then find the one that comes next. Keep going all the way around. Here’s a hint: the circle never really ends.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word. Act out metamorphosis: curl up small, then open your arms like wings.

part1.label: Part 1 · every living thing has a life cycle

part2.label: Part 2 · side by side (Clue 2)
part2.script: Two babies hatched on the same day: a monarch caterpillar and a lubber grasshopper. Drag the slider and watch them grow up side by side. Stop at each day listed under the slider. Which baby already looks like its mom and dad? Which one looks like a totally different animal?

part3.label: Part 3 · close the circle (Clue 3)
part3.script: Every life cycle is a circle. I put the first stage on for you. Drag the next one onto the glowing spot, and keep going until the circle closes. Then decide what kind of life cycle it is. Count the stages. That’s a big hint.

explore.label: Part 4 · alike and different (Clue 4)
explore.script: Scientists compare. Pick a pair, then sort each fact: true for only one of them, or true for both? When you finish the monarch and the dragonfly, look closely at the dragonfly’s side. It might explain those shells on my cattails.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: are my shells dead bugs, and what is that green case? Then answer two questions, write one Florida life cycle, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

partc.label: Part C · a Florida life cycle

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says a caterpillar and a butterfly are completely different animals. They don’t even look alike! Hmm. Think about the chrysalis on my milkweed. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed! My shells weren’t dead bugs. They were dragonfly skins, and the green case was a monarch chrysalis. Next time, winter is coming to the pond. Where do the dragonflies and the monarchs go? We’ll find out.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how animals notice and respond?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A dragonfly nymph climbs out of the pond and sheds its skin one last time.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “dragonfly nymph”, “sheds” and “skin”. Those words tell who and what happens. Small words like “the” and “of” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.

why.t: A net on a long pole that scientists sweep through ponds and streams to catch small water animals, look at them, and let them go.

parts.t: The flat side sits on the pond bottom, so animals can’t escape underneath.

dnymph.name: Dragonfly nymph
dnymph.alt: A brown dragonfly nymph with six legs and no wings.
dnymph.note: It lives underwater and grabs food with a jaw that shoots out. One day it will climb a cattail, shed its skin one last time, and fly away as a dragonfly.

mayfly.name: Mayfly nymph
mayfly.alt: A thin mayfly nymph with feathery gills along its sides and three tails.
mayfly.note: Feathery gills on its sides help it breathe underwater. Mayflies go through incomplete metamorphosis too.

tadpole.name: Tadpole
tadpole.alt: Two brown tadpoles with round bodies and long tails.
tadpole.note: A young frog. Frogs change shape too: the tadpole grows legs and loses its tail. But frogs aren’t insects.

snail.name: Ramshorn snail
snail.alt: Two ramshorn snails with flat, coiled shells on a plant stem.
snail.note: Baby ramshorn snails hatch from eggs already shaped like tiny snails. No metamorphosis: they just grow.

q.q: Which animal from your tray will one day leave an empty shell on a cattail?

opts.why: Yes! It climbs out of the water, and the adult crawls out of its old skin. Now gently pour the tray back into the pond.
Snails don’t climb out and shed their skin. Which animal becomes a flying insect?
A tadpole becomes a frog, not a shell on a cattail. Which one becomes a dragonfly?
